title: Two Hundred Years of Psychiatry's Lessons: No Penicillin, Only Trial and Error
dek: From ice-pick lobotomies to insulin coma, psychiatry repeatedly claimed 80% cure rates, yet never found a psychiatric penicillin—even today's best drugs still see eight in ten patients drop out of trials.
why: The first half is psychiatry's dark history, the second half is how drugs and diagnosis were shaped by commerce and hope; dense but worth the patience.
who: Founders, investors and engineers interested in medical history, psychopharmacology, and how science gets distorted by commerce and hope.

points.body: Modern psychopharmacology was born in the early 1950s, and Andrew Scull stresses this was not a planned achievement but a "serendipitous event," almost purely accidental. It was indeed an advance over psychiatry's earlier tools, but the drugs we have today are only symptomatic treatment, not cures—"we do not have any psychiatric penicillin." Worse is the iatrogenic harm: making PTSD patients confront their trauma often makes things worse for many; antipsychotics and antidepressants are at best partially effective, and doctors cannot tell in advance who will respond and who will deteriorate, while those in between must weigh side effects against efficacy.

points.h: Twenty billion dollars bought not one bit of improvement
points.body: Under Stephen Hyman and Thomas Insel, the NIMH invested in mental illness as brain disease, betting heavily on genetics and neuroscience. After leaving office, Insel admitted in an MIT interview: they funded a lot of cool science, but after spending $20 billion, the situation of mental illness patients had "improved not one bit." Scull calls this a devastating admission. The DSM-5 originally aimed to rewrite the diagnostic system based on underlying pathology, but by around 2008 the editors gave up and fell back on the 1980 approach; before publication, Insel and Hyman publicly denounced it as unscientific and useless, and Spitzer and Alan Francis also fiercely criticized its backroom dealings.

points.h: America's largest psychiatric wards are prisons
points.body: People with severe mental illness live on average 15 to 25 years less than others, and the gap is widening. Scull attributes much of this to public policy rather than psychiatry itself: today the three largest inpatient psychiatric "centers" in the US are the Los Angeles County Jail, Chicago's Cook County Jail, and New York's Rikers Island. Patients cycle through a three-stage loop—brief hospitalization, the streets or cheap motels, prison. Community care is what Scull calls "a shell game without a P," a con with no alternative facilities, amounting to a return to some dark age.

points.h: If you can't cure them, blame their genes
points.body: Early asylums were born of intense optimism; the earliest alienists believed that if patients came early, 60%, 70%, even 80% could be cured. Actual discharge rates were only 35% to 40%, so each year a cohort of chronic patients accumulated, the ratio of new to chronic patients worsened, and the asylum's image was defined by that chronic patient who "only left in a pine box." By the late 19th century, the cure rate by in-house count was only 10% to 12%. Faced with the charge "you promised and failed," the answer turned to blaming the victim: mental illness was a fundamental biological defect, patients were evolutionary throwbacks, degenerates, who could not be released because "they breed like rabbits." This narrative justified lifelong confinement and sterilization.

points.h: Ice-pick lobotomy: psychiatry won a Nobel Prize
points.body: Walter Freeman began performing lobotomies in 1936, building on the work of Portuguese neurologist Egas Moniz the year before, for which Moniz won the 1949 Nobel Prize in Medicine—by then he had 14 years of experience. Freeman wanted to be the Henry Ford of lobotomy, mechanizing the operation: first electroshock to render the patient unconscious, then driving an ice pick through the eye socket into the skull, stirring and cutting. He toured state hospitals in a van he called the "lobotomobile," switching from right hand to left when tired, sometimes doing 20 to 30 cases in an afternoon, and boasted he could teach any fool to do a lobotomy in 20 minutes, "even a psychiatrist"—he was a neurologist and held psychiatrists in contempt. The operation was performed from the 1930s into the early 1970s, finally fading through generational turnover and antipsychotic drugs.

points.h: Cotton cut out patients' stomachs, claimed 80% cured
points.body: Henry Cotton was a psychiatrist trained by Emil Kraepelin and Adolf Meyer, who ran the New Jersey State Hospital in Trenton. He embraced the theory of "focal sepsis": low-grade infection releases toxins in the body, and when the toxins reach the brain they poison it. With no antibiotics, the solution was to find the source and cut it out—first pull teeth, patient not better; then remove tonsils, still not better; so remove stomach, spleen, colon, and claim 80% of patients cured. Wealthy patients came from all over the country. He gave a lecture series at Princeton, published by Oxford University Press and Princeton University Press, and The New York Times called it a major breakthrough. In reality, 45% of those who underwent abdominal surgery died within a year. He died of a heart attack in 1933, and his successor stopped abdominal surgery, but tooth extraction and tonsillectomy continued until 1960—a dentist who arrived in 1916 pulled hundreds of thousands of teeth and firmly believed Cotton should have won a Nobel Prize.

points.h: Schizophrenia may not be a disease at all
points.body: After the genome was decoded, people expected to quickly find Mendelian genes for schizophrenia, but it did not happen. Now with genome-wide association studies, adding up 300 small genomic variants explains only about 10% of schizophrenia—Scull's assessment: "not very powerful." More troubling, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and autism overlap heavily in genetic abnormalities, undermining disease classifications based on symptomatology. He cites British psychiatrist Robin Murray: schizophrenia is more like the extreme end of psychosis, a continuum. He speculates that if in ten years psychiatry announced "there is no such thing as schizophrenia," public trust in psychiatry would be severely damaged.

points.h: New drugs no better than old, eight in ten quit trials
points.body: The CATIE study (published in the New England Journal of Medicine) compared one first-generation antipsychotic with four newer ones and concluded the new drugs were no more effective than the old. The more underappreciated finding was tolerability: depending on the drug, 67% to 82% of patients dropped out of the trial, either because the drug did not work or the side effects were unbearable. That is, these are already "our best drugs," yet real-world discontinuation rates are astonishingly high. Old drugs are off-patent and cheap; second-generation ones are patented and expensive, in some cases 10 times more, but the higher price bought no efficacy advantage.
